Certified type:
- Category: Load cell
- Type designations: SLC820..., PDX... — "Type : SLC820... or PDX..." Hmm, the "..." here might indicate variants. Type designations: ["SLC820", "PDX"]? The markdown says "Type : SLC820... or PDX...". The "..." could be part of the designation (e.g. SLC820-XXX variants). I'll record as "SLC820..." and "PDX..."? Actually more likely the "..." indicates that additional suffixes exist. Safer to record "SLC820..." and "PDX..." as literally written? Hmm. Let me think. The certificate says "Type: SLC820... or PDX...". I think these are family prefixes. I'll use "SLC820" and "PDX" as type_designations. Actually to be safe, keep literal: "SLC820...", "PDX...". Hmm, "Don't fabricate" — the literal text is "SLC820... or PDX...". I'll record ["SLC820", "PDX"] since the ellipsis indicates variability. Actually, many OIML certs write "SLC820..." meaning series. I'll keep the literal "SLC820..." and "PDX..." — hmm. I think cleaner: "SLC820", "PDX". I'll go with literal including ellipsis? The rule says "all type/model identifiers mentioned". The identifiers are SLC820 and PDX with ellipsis denoting series. I'll use "SLC820" and "PDX".

- Module designation: "Analog load cell"? The cert says "compression load cell, with strain gauges, equipped with electronics". Under R60, module designation for load cells is "Analog load cell" or "Digital load cell". With electronics... Hmm. The certificate doesn't explicitly say "Analog load cell". It says "A compression load cell, with strain gauges, equipped with electronics". I could set module_designation to null or infer. Rule: don't fabricate. The schema says module_designation: "Analog load cell" | "Not applicable" | null. Since it's not stated explicitly, set null. Actually "equipped with electronics" — under R60-2000, load cells with electronics... The characteristics include "Software identification 2.xx" which suggests digital/electronic. But not explicit "digital load cell". I'll leave null.

- Description: "compression load cell, with strain gauges, equipped with electronics"

Model family: The characteristics table has two capacity ranges as columns:
- Column 1: Emax 20 t up to and including 90 t — n=6000, Y=25000, Z=6000, safe overload 200% of Emax
- Column 2: Emax 100 t up to and including 500 t — n=3000, Y=10000, Z=3000, safe overload 150% of Emax

So this is a config/model axis: capacity range. Two "models": Emax 20–90 t and Emax 100–500 t. I'll model as model_family with models "Emax=20t-90t" and "Emax=100t-500t", or use config_level. Actually it's a range, not discrete values. The axis is the capacity range. I think config_level fits: attribute varies by capacity range. But model_family with two models is also reasonable. Hmm.

The rules: matrix detection — models vary per model. Here there are two groups based on Emax range. I'll use model_family with two models:
- model_id: "Emax=20t-90t"
- model_id: "Emax=100t-500t"

And model_level characteristics:
- maximum_capacity (Emax): {min: 20, max: 90} t and {min: 100, max: 500} t
- max_load_cell_intervals_n: 6000 / 3000 (footnote 1)
- ratio_y_emax_over_vmin: 25000 / 10000 (footnote 1)
- ratio_z_emax_over_dr: 6000 / 3000 (footnote 1) — formula Z = Emax/(2*DR)
- safe_overload: 200 % of Emax / 150 % of Emax

Type-level characteristics:
- minimum_dead_load: 50 kg
- accuracy_class: C
- temperature_range: {min: -10, max: 40} °C
- fraction_plc: 0.8
- humidity_class: CH
- recommended_excitation: {min: 7.5, max: 24} V DC — "7,5 V – 24 V DC" → split: recommended_excitation_voltage {min: 7.5, max: 24} V, and maybe power_supply_type DC. Hmm, "7,5 V – 24 V DC" — I'd record recommended_excitation_voltage: {min: 7.5, max: 24}, unit V, and excitation_type: "DC"? The max excitation is "24 V DC" → excitation_maximum: 24 V. I'll record:
  - recommended_excitation_voltage: {min: 7.5, max: 24}, "V"
  - excitation_maximum: 24, "V"
  Maybe include "DC" as excitation_type: "DC". That could be noise; I'll include as a simple value for excitation type? The rule 3 example splits "110-240V AC 50/60Hz". Here "7,5 V – 24 V DC". I'll add "excitation_type": "DC". Fine.
- transducer_material: Stainless steel
- atmospheric_protection: Hermetically welded
- electromagnetic_environment_class: E2
- number_of_counts_for_emax: "≥ Y * 5 / p_LC" — formula string: "Y * 5 / pLC". Value as string "Y*5/pLC". Hmm, "≥ Y * 5 / pLC" — keep as string "Y*5/pLC". I'll write value: "Y * 5 / pLC", unit null.
- software_identification: "2.xx" with footnote 2.

Footnotes:
- 1) — "The characteristics for n_max, Y and Z can be reduced separately." Wait — the remarks say "1. The characteristics for nmax, Y and Z can be reduced separately. 2. xx is a number between 00 and 99 representing updates of the non legally relevant part of the software."

These are remarks, numbered 1 and 2. Footnote markers in table: (1) on n, Y, Z; (2) on 2.xx. So footnotes:
- marker "1)": text "The characteristics for nmax, Y and Z can be reduced separately."
- marker "2)": text "xx is a number between 00 and 99 representing updates of the non legally relevant part of the software."

Recommendation:
- id: R60
- edition: 2000
- amendment: null
- scheme: A
- accuracy_classes: ["C"]

Also the US national requirements: NIST Handbook 44, NCWM Publication 14, accuracy class III L. That's additional national requirements — not part of the recommendation accuracy classes? The schema for recommendation.accuracy_classes — the main recommendation accuracy class is C. The US addition says "Accuracy class III L". Could record accuracy_classes: ["C"] and maybe mention US in... there's no field for national requirements. Could put in matrix_tables? No. Maybe just leave accuracy_classes: ["C", "IIIL"]? Hmm. The certificate attests conformity with R60 for accuracy class C; additionally complies with US requirements incl. class III L. I think accuracy_classes: ["C"] is canonical for the R60 recommendation; but including "III L" is informative. The schema says accuracy_classes[] under recommendation. I'll include ["C"] only, since III L is a US national requirement, not OIML R60 class. Hmm, but NIST HB44 classes are like III L. To not lose info... there's no field. I could skip. Actually I could include both: ["C", "III L"] — but that conflates. I'll keep ["C"]. Maybe record the US requirements in description? Not needed. I'll leave it.

Test reports:
- R60/2000-NL1-09.08, dated 11 June 2009, 53 pages, role: type_evaluation_report
- NMi-15200551-01, dated 15 April 2016, 15 pages, role: test_report
- NMi-2611823-02, dated 13 May 2022, 23 pages, role: test_report

Revision history:
- revision "0", date 2019-06-26, changes null (the change column is "-")
- revision "1", date 2022-05-13, changes "Updated main board, Additional EMC test done"

Certificate date_issued: 13 May 2022 → format? Probably ISO "2022-05-13". The revision history shows 2022-05-13 for revision 1. Use "2022-05-13".

certificate.number: "R60/2000-A-NL1-19-07" and revision 1. The schema has number, and revision_history. Maybe number should be just the base number. I'll set number: "R60/2000-A-NL1-19-07". Some include revision in number; there's revision_history for that. Keep number without revision.

Now the model family. The two capacity ranges: 20 t up to and including 90 t; 100 t up to and including 500 t.

model_family:
- family_name: null (or "SLC820 / PDX"? not explicit). null.
- models: [{"model_id": "Emax=20t-90t"}, {"model_id": "Emax=100t-500t"}]

Hmm, but the actual type designations are SLC820 and PDX. Maybe models should be based on ranges since characteristics vary by range. The model_level entries reference model ids. I'll use "Emax=20t-90t" and "Emax=100t-500t".

model_level characteristics:
1. maximum_capacity (Emax):
   - {"model": "Emax=20t-90t", "value": {"min": 20, "max": 90}, "unit_symbol": "t"}
   - {"model": "Emax=100t-500t", "value": {"min": 100, "max": 500}, "unit_symbol": "t"}
2. max_load_cell_intervals_n (footnote 1):
   - 6000, 3000
3. ratio_y_emax_over_vmin (footnote 1):
   - 25000, 10000
4. ratio_z_emax_over_dr (footnote 1):
   - 6000, 3000
5. safe_overload:
   - 200 % (reference Emax), 150 % (reference Emax)

Wait — the labels: "Ratio of minimum LC Verification interval (1) Y = Emax/Vmin" → canonical: ratio_y_emax_over_vmin. "Ratio of minimum dead load output return (1) Z = Emax/(2*DR)" → ratio_z_emax_over_dr.

"Maximum number of load cell intervals (n)" → max_load_cell_intervals_n. The schema example: `max_load_cell_intervals_nlc` for "Max. number of load cell intervals n_LC". Here it's "(n)" so max_load_cell_intervals_n.

Safe overload: "200 % of Emax" → value 200, unit "%", plus safe_overload_reference "Emax". Per rule 3. Since it's model_level with two values, I'll add attribute "safe_overload" with unit "%" and a separate type_level characteristic "safe_overload_reference": {"value": "Emax"}. Or just include the value as string "200% of Emax"? Better structured: unit "%" value 200, footnote none, and a reference characteristic.

Actually since both models reference Emax, safe_overload_reference: {value: "Emax", unit_symbol: null, unit_id: null} at type_level.

Values with footnote markers in model_level: {"model": ..., "value": ..., "footnote_markers": ["1)"]}. Also unit_symbol at the attribute level (as in example: "unit_symbol": "t" at the model_level entry level). The example shows unit_symbol at attribute level in model_level. Good.

Structured values need unit_symbol/unit_id per value? The schema example for model_level: {"attribute": "qmax", "unit_symbol": "m³/h", "values": [{"model": "G1.6", "value": 2.5}, ...]}. So unit at attribute level. For value objects with footnote_markers, they show {"model": "Emax=25t", "value": 25} without footnote structure; but rule 7 shows footnote_markers on values. I'll do values: [{"model": "...", "value": 6000, "footnote_markers": ["1)"]}].

For the Emax value being a range: value {"min": 20, "max": 90}.

Type-level characteristics — each value must be an object with value, unit_symbol, unit_id:

- minimum_dead_load: {value: 50, unit_symbol: "kg", unit_id: null}
- accuracy_class: {value: "C", unit_symbol: null, unit_id: null}

- excitation_type: {value: "DC"} — maybe fold into recommended? I'll include separately? The original "7,5 V – 24 V DC" and "24 V DC". I'll add "excitation_type": {"value": "DC"}. Hmm, maybe overkill but harmless. Actually rule 3's example explicitly splits AC type. I'll include.

- transducer_material: {value: "Stainless steel"}
- atmospheric_protection: {value: "Hermetically welded"}

- software_identification: {value: "2.xx", footnote_markers: ["2)"]}
- safe_overload_reference: {value: "Emax"}

unit_id: leave null everywhere (rule says leave null unless certain). °C — could be "u:degree_Celsius" but instruction says leave null unless certain; the examples show it, but I'm not certain of exact IDs, keep null.

category: "Load cell".

description: "Compression load cell, with strain gauges, equipped with electronics" — from "A compression load cell, with strain gauges, equipped with electronics".

Components: none named. Skip.
